title: How close were your length estimates?
description: Five objects are guessed and then measured, and the sample lengths are drawn as a double-bar graph. The positive difference for each object is found, and the average difference tells how close the guesses were.
teaching_notes: One idea: take each difference as a positive number before finding the average, so that guesses that are too long and too short do not cancel. Watch for children who subtract in the same order each time and get negative values.

video_script.why: The child can find a mean and draw a double-bar graph and now measures how accurate guesses are.
video_script.substitution: The mean of the positive differences shows the typical size of the mistake.
video_script.anchor: Sample data (cm), estimate then measure: pen 14 and 15, eraser 5 and 4.5, palm 16 and 17.5, geometry box 18 and 16, notebook 25 and 27
video_script.payoff_line: The sample estimates were off by one point four centimetres on average.

final_answer.value: For the sample data the average difference is 1.4 cm
final_answer.spoken: the sample estimates were off by one point four centimetres on average

maths_rules: sample data, labelled sample: pen 14 / 15, eraser 5 / 4.5, palm 16 / 17.5, box 18 / 16, notebook 25 / 27
double-bar graph: largest value 27, 1 unit = 5 cm, 6 units reach 30; heights = value ÷ 5: 2.8 and 3, 1 and 0.9, 3.2 and 3.5, 3.6 and 3.2, 5 and 5.4
video_script.design: One small table of five objects and two columns. Each row gets a positive difference, then the ten bars are drawn in pairs.
open_questions: The book asks the viewer to estimate and measure real objects, so the ten lengths are sample data from the worklist and are labelled sample on screen.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; a pen, an eraser, a palm, a geometry box and a notebook lined up beside a ruler

marks.m1: the title card From your book appears
marks.m3: a ruler slides under each object

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>You guess the length of five objects, such as a pen and an eraser.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Then you measure each one with a ruler.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>How can we say how close the guesses were?

beats.on_screen: the five objects and the ruler stay on the board

marks.m1: Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a close guess before measuring labelled estimate; the gap between two numbers, taken as positive, labelled positive difference; average of those gaps

marks.m1: a close guess before measuring is labelled estimate
marks.m2: the gap between an estimate and a measure is drawn and labelled positive difference
marks.m3: the gaps are added and divided by their number
marks.m4: the hint line the same way as the book's example glows

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>A close guess made before measuring is called an estimate.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The gap between two numbers, always taken as positive, is called the positive difference.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The average of the gaps tells how close the guesses were.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>We solve it the same way as the example in your book.

beats.on_screen: Given (sample), in cm, estimate then measure: pen 14, 15; eraser 5, 4.5; palm 16, 17.5; geometry box 18, 16; notebook 25, 27

marks.m1: the word sample and the table appear
marks.m2: the eraser and palm rows glow
marks.m3: the geometry box and notebook rows glow

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, five objects with an estimate and then a measure, in centimetres. The pen is fourteen and fifteen.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The eraser is five and four point five. The palm is sixteen and seventeen point five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The geometry box is eighteen and sixteen. The notebook is twenty five and twenty seven.

beats.on_screen: To find: a double-bar graph; the average difference between estimates and measures

marks.m1: the two tasks are written one under the other

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to draw a double-bar graph and find the average difference between the estimates and the measures.

beats.on_screen: positive differences: pen 15 - 14 = 1; eraser 5 - 4.5 = 0.5; palm 17.5 - 16 = 1.5; geometry box 18 - 16 = 2; notebook 27 - 25 = 2

marks.m1: the greater value minus the smaller value is written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, find the positive difference for each object. Take the smaller value from the greater one.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>For the pen, fifteen take away fourteen is one. For the eraser, five take away four point five is zero point five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>For the palm, it is one point five. For the geometry box, it is two. For the notebook, it is two.

marks.m1: the five differences line up in a column

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, add the five positive differences.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One, zero point five, one point five, two and two add up to seven.

beats.on_screen: largest value 27; 1 unit = 5 cm; 6 units reach 30; height = value ÷ 5: pen 2.8 and 3; eraser 1 and 0.9; palm 3.2 and 3.5; geometry box 3.6 and 3.2; notebook 5 and 5.4

marks.m2: 1 unit = 5 cm is written and the line is marked to 30

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, choose a scale for the graph. The largest value is twenty seven.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Let one unit stand for five centimetres. Six units reach thirty, which is enough.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Each bar's height is its value divided by five.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The notebook's measure is twenty seven divided by five, which is five point four units.

beats.on_screen: the double-bar graph: an estimate bar and a measure bar for each object, with a key

marks.m2: the measure bars grow beside them

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, draw an estimate bar for each object.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Draw a measure bar beside it.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Add a key to tell the two kinds of bar apart.

beats.on_screen: check the total in the opposite order: 2 + 2 + 1.5 + 1 + 0.5 = 7

marks.m1: the differences are added again from the greatest to the least

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step five, check the total by adding the differences again in the opposite order.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two, two, one point five, one and zero point five also make seven.

beats.on_screen: Answer (sample): average difference = 7 ÷ 5 = 1.4 cm; repeat with your own objects

marks.m3: the words estimate first, then measure appear

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The average difference is the total divided by the number of objects. Seven divided by five is one point four.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The sample estimates were off by one point four centimetres on average.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Repeat with your own objects. Estimate first, then measure.
